children: The U.S. Treasury’s expanded debt-buyback program may be encountering limits just as policymakers debate Federal Reserve interest-rate policy, persistent inflation and the government’s growing financing needs.

Treasury accepted $5.2 billion of securities during its first buyback operation with a maximum size of $6 billion, according to a Sept. 11 report by Subadra Rajappa, head of U.S. rates strategy at Société Générale. Investors submitted $10.5 billion of offers, producing a cover ratio of about two times.
That was the weakest cover ratio recorded since the program began and far below the ratios of nine to 10 times commonly seen during much of 2025, Rajappa said.

Treasury had justified increasing the maximum operation size by pointing to consistently strong participation and the large volume of attractive offers it received in longer-dated securities. The initial results suggest that participation did not grow fast enough to support a tripling of the buyback limit.
Treasury buys a wider range of bonds
The composition of the operation may be more revealing than its relatively low cover ratio.

Treasury accepted offers involving 23 of the 40 eligible securities, compared with roughly three issues during a typical previous operation. The purchases included nine securities that had never before been bought through the program.

Earlier operations had concentrated heavily on a small group of older 20-year Treasury bonds. The much broader selection could represent a deliberate change in strategy. It also could indicate that Treasury had to cast a wider net to approach its enlarged target.

The next buyback involving 20-year to 30-year securities is scheduled for Sept. 24. Rajappa said that operation will help determine whether the latest results were an isolated adjustment or evidence that larger buybacks require Treasury to purchase from a structurally broader group of securities.
Investor significance

For bond investors, the results raise doubts about Treasury’s ability to use buybacks as a powerful or easily scalable tool for supporting liquidity in the long-term debt market. If participation remains limited, Treasury may have to accept less favorable prices, conduct smaller operations or alter the amount and maturity of the debt it issues.

Those choices could influence long-term Treasury yields, the shape of the yield curve and borrowing costs throughout the economy. Mortgage rates, corporate financing costs and equity valuations are all sensitive to changes in long-term government yields.

Buybacks do not necessarily reduce the federal debt. Treasury generally finances the purchases by issuing other securities. The program is intended mainly to improve market liquidity and manage the composition of outstanding debt.
Pressure builds on the 20-year bond
Rajappa sees the 20-year Treasury bond
as the most likely candidate for an issuance reduction when the government announces its November refunding plans.

The maturity has struggled to develop a reliable investor base since Treasury reintroduced it in 2020. Former Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin also suggested in 2024 that the government should consider eliminating the 20-year bond because of its comparatively high financing costs.

Société Générale argues that Treasury’s buyback activity is effectively illuminating the 20-year sector’s persistent weaknesses. Buying back older bonds could provide a gradual way to reduce the amount outstanding while preparing the market for smaller future auctions.

If Treasury wants to exert greater influence over long-term yields, Rajappa said changes to issuance may ultimately prove more effective than increasingly large buyback operations. The November refunding announcement could therefore become an important test of whether officials are prepared to reduce the supply of 20-year debt.
